title_en: Open-Plan Offices Are an Expensive Mistake
description_ru: Резкая критика офисов открытой планировки: почему они снижают концентрацию и общение и почему компании держатся за них ради экономии.
text:
Some years ago, I worked for a company that tore down every wall on its fourth floor. The executives called it a transformation. The consultants who designed it called it a "collaborative ecosystem", and a bright banner in the lobby promised that it would unlock our creativity. What it unlocked, as far as I could tell, was a great many noise-cancelling headphones. Within a month, my colleagues had stopped talking to one another and begun communicating, with a kind of weary irony, by sending each other messages across a distance of three metres.

I have since spent a good deal of time asking why this pattern keeps repeating, and I have reached a conclusion that is not particularly flattering to my fellow managers. The open-plan office was never really about collaboration. It was about cost. A room without partitions can hold more desks per square metre, and in cities where rent is the second-largest expense after salaries, the appeal of squeezing in an extra fifteen per cent of staff is difficult to resist. The language of creativity and togetherness was a decorative coat of paint on a spreadsheet.

If open-plan advocates were right, we should expect to see a surge in face-to-face interaction. We do not. In a much-quoted study carried out by two Harvard researchers, employees at two multinational companies were tracked with sensors before and after the move to open space. The result startled everyone except, presumably, the employees: face-to-face conversation fell by roughly seventy per cent, while email and instant messaging rose sharply. People, it turns out, do not enjoy having intimate discussions in full view of thirty colleagues, so they retreat to the only private space left to them, which is the screen.

The trouble goes beyond the loss of conversation. Cognitive psychologists have established, repeatedly and over decades, that background speech is uniquely disruptive to tasks that involve reading, writing or reasoning. Unlike a steady hum of machinery, which the brain learns to tune out, intelligible words attract involuntary attention. We cannot help it; our minds are tuned to decode language. An open-plan office thus gives us the worst possible acoustic environment for the kind of thinking that employers claim to value most.

Nor is it merely a matter of concentration. Anyone who has worked in such a space will recognise the subtle theatre of being permanently observed. You hesitate before taking a personal call, even a quick one to the dentist. You feel a flicker of guilt when you lean back to think, because staring out of the window might look like idleness. You become reluctant to speak candidly, and you wonder whether your colleague's cough is a sign of illness that you will inherit by Thursday. Studies have found that employees in open-plan offices take more sick days, an unsurprising result when one considers the quantity of shared air.

Defenders of the arrangement tend to make three arguments, and they deserve a fair hearing. The first is that it fosters spontaneous encounters, the chance conversation at the coffee machine that leads to a brilliant idea. This is not nonsense; serendipity matters. But it is the layout of shared spaces, not the abolition of private ones, that produces serendipity, and a well-placed kitchen does the work far more effectively than a hundred desks in a hall.

The second argument is generational: young employees, we are told, prefer open spaces and find them energising. I am sceptical. When I have asked younger colleagues, they frequently say that they enjoy the social atmosphere in their first month and long for a quiet corner in their second. Sociability and privacy are not enemies. A good workplace offers both, and lets people choose.

The third argument is that open-plan offices flatten hierarchy by showing that managers sit among their teams. This has a certain egalitarian charm, though in practice the manager usually retains a meeting room for confidential discussions and the staff are left with the noise. A truly democratic office would give everybody access to the same quiet room, not deprive everybody of one.

What would I propose instead? I am not nostalgic for the windowless cubicle, which had its own special miseries. The best offices I have visited use what architects call activity-based design: a mixture of small enclosed rooms for focused work, comfortable lounges for informal talk, a few larger spaces for teams that need to spread out, and, crucially, a genuine right to work somewhere else, including at home, when the task demands it. Such an arrangement costs more per head than a warehouse of desks, but it is cheaper than the alternative.

For the alternative has hidden costs that never appear on the property budget. A single interruption can take twenty minutes to recover from, according to researchers who have studied how long it takes to resume a complex task. Multiply that by several interruptions per person per day, then by hundreds of employees, and the savings on rent look rather thin. Companies that boast of efficiency are, I suspect, paying a premium in lost concentration, higher absenteeism and quiet resignations.

I should say, in fairness, that I have also worked in a lovely open space where the culture was considerate, the sound was well absorbed by carpets and fabric panels, and each person had a place to withdraw. It can be done. But it is done rarely, and almost never by those who adopt open plan for the sake of the spreadsheet. If you are an executive who is about to knock down some walls, I beg you to ask yourself one question first: are you trying to help your people to think, or are you only trying to fit more of them into the room?

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Короткий, расслабленный i, не как русское «и»: губы не растянуты, язык чуть ниже.
Начинайте со сложенных в трубочку губ, как для у; не подменяйте на в.
В конце слога язык касается альвеол кончиком, а спинка отходит назад: smaLL, weLL.
collAborative, serenDIpity: в длинных словах ударение ближе к середине, на 2–3 слоге.

questions.question: What was the real reason for open-plan offices, according to the writer?
questions.answer: Cost: they fit more desks into less space.

questions.question: What did the Harvard study find?
questions.answer: Face-to-face conversation fell by about seventy per cent.

questions.question: Why is background speech so disruptive?
questions.answer: The brain involuntarily tries to decode intelligible words.

questions.question: What kind of office does the writer prefer?
questions.answer: Activity-based design with quiet rooms, lounges and the right to work elsewhere.
